questionText:
Read the following hazardous materials and informal industrial economy case study and answer the questions that follow:

Seelampur, a densely populated low-income neighborhood in North East Delhi, is recognized as one of the largest informal electronic waste (e-waste) processing hubs in Asia. Every day, truckloads of obsolete computers, mobile phones, printed circuit boards (PCBs), and cathode ray tubes (CRTs) arrive from across India. Operating in narrow residential alleys without any personal protective equipment, ventilation, or regulatory oversight, informal workers—many of them women and children—manually dismantle electronic hardware. To extract valuable precious metals (such as Gold, Silver, and Copper), workers heat circuit boards over open kerosene burners to desolder components, inhaling dense fumes of lead (Pb) and toxic polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE flame retardants). Circuit board scrap is then immersed in primitive open-air chemical baths of concentrated nitric acid and aqua regia (acid leaching) on rooftops to strip copper and gold. The spent, highly acidic leaching sludges containing lethal concentrations of cyanide, lead, cadmium, and mercury are dumped directly into unlined open gutters that discharge into the Yamuna river. Blood tests of informal e-waste workers reveal alarming blood lead levels exceeding 40 ug/dL (far above the CDC action level of 5 ug/dL), severe respiratory impairment, kidney tubular damage, and irreversible neurological disorders.

Question: Old television sets and CRT computer monitors dismantled in informal yards are hazardous primarily because their funnel glass contains large quantities of:

options.text: Barium oxide used to enhance optical clarity and phosphorescent luminescence
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Inverts the governing property or boundary condition.

options.text: Cadmium sulfide applied as a high-voltage coating on inner phosphor screens
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

options.text: Lead oxide (PbO) integrated to shield viewers from internal X-ray radiation
options.mistakeAnalysis: Correct answer. Accurately identifies the verified NCERT principle for Cathode Ray Tube (CRT) Toxic Constituent.

options.text: Polybrominated biphenyls integrated as thermal flame retardants in the casing
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Confuses related NCERT concepts or attributes.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
According to NCERT principles for Environmental Pollution (Cathode Ray Tube (CRT) Toxic Constituent):
Lead oxide (PbO) integrated to shield viewers from internal X-ray radiation

Detailed Analysis:
CRT glass contains up to 2–3 kg of lead oxide to block cathode X-rays; crushing CRTs in open yards releases toxic lead dust into ambient air and soil. Hence, Option D is correct.

Therefore, option (C) is the correct answer.

questionText:
Read the following riverine pollution and urban hydrology case study and answer the questions that follow:

The 22-kilometer stretch of the Yamuna River passing through the National Capital Territory of Delhi—from the Wazirabad barrage down to the Okhla barrage—accounts for less than 2% of the river's total length, yet contributes over 76% of the river's total pollution load. Upstream of Delhi, almost the entire fresh river flow is diverted at Hathnikund Barrage in Haryana for irrigation canals and municipal drinking water. As a result, the river enters Delhi at Wazirabad with virtually zero fresh environmental baseflow (E-flow) during non-monsoon months. Within Delhi, 22 major un-trapped municipal storm drains (including the infamous Najafgarh and Shahdara drains) discharge over 3,500 million liters per day (MLD) of untreated and partially treated sewage, industrial tanneries effluent, and chemical waste directly into the dry riverbed. During festival seasons, dramatic images of thick, white, toxic foam floating on the river at Kalindi Kunj and Okhla barrage make international headlines. Environmental chemists determined that the toxic frothing is caused by high concentrations of non-biodegradable surfactants from household detergents, industrial phosphate builders, and decaying organic matter. When wastewater plunges over the Okhla barrage gates, mechanical aeration and turbulence churn the surfactant-rich water into persistent, billowing foam containing pathogenic bacteria and heavy metals. Dissolved oxygen along this entire stretch remains at 0 mg/L throughout non-monsoon months, rendering the river ecologically dead.

Question: What is the characteristic Dissolved Oxygen (DO) level measured by CPCB across the Yamuna from Wazirabad to Okhla during non-monsoon months?

options.text: 5.0 mg/L (Safe outdoor bathing standard)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Inverts the governing property or boundary condition.

options.text: 0 mg/L (Absolute anoxia, supporting zero aquatic fish life)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Correct answer. Accurately identifies the verified NCERT principle for Dissolved Oxygen in Delhi Yamuna.

options.text: 14.0 mg/L (Super-saturated pristine water)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

options.text: 8.0 mg/L (Optimal drinking water quality)
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Confuses related NCERT concepts or attributes.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
According to NCERT principles for Environmental Pollution (Dissolved Oxygen in Delhi Yamuna):
0 mg/L (Absolute anoxia, supporting zero aquatic fish life)

Detailed Analysis:
Continuous sewage discharges consume all available oxygen, keeping DO at 0 mg/L along the 22-km Delhi stretch throughout the dry season.
Hence, Option A is correct.

Therefore, option (B) is the correct answer.

questionText:
Match the waste processing technology in List I with its operational mechanism in List II:

List I:
(A) Windrow Composting
(B) Vermicomposting
(C) Incineration (Mass Burn)
(D) Pyrolysis

List II:
(I) Aerobic biological decomposition of segregated organic waste piled in elongated triangular heaps turned regularly
(II) Biological composting utilizing specialized surface-dwelling epigeic earthworms (e.g., Eisenia fetida)
(III) Controlled high-temperature thermal combustion (850–1,100 degrees Celsius) in excess oxygen, generating steam electricity
(IV) Thermal decomposition of carbonaceous waste at elevated temperatures in the total absence of oxygen, yielding bio-oil and syngas

questionText:

(I) Ingestion of arsenic-contaminated water over 2 to 5 years with cumulative body burden accumulation
(II) Appearance of melanosis (spotted dark pigmentation on chest and limbs) and diffuse keratosis
(III) Hyperkeratosis: thickening, nodular roughness, and painful cracked fissures on palms and soles
